strengths: Systematic and fairly comprehensive empirical exploration: the paper trains Mamba-based HuBERT variants (causal Mamba, ExtBiMamba, InnBiMamba, with/without MLP) and compares them against matched Transformer baselines across fine-tuning (long-context ASR, causal/streaming ASR) and probing (SUPERB subset), plus representational analyses (phone purity, CCA), which is more unified than prior single-task studies of Mamba in speech.

The efficiency analysis is concrete and well-motivated: MACs/second and RTF measured over 5s-320s inputs, averaged over 10 runs on specified hardware, clearly demonstrating near-constant compute for Mamba vs. quadratic growth and OOM for causal Transformers beyond 80s.

Honest and balanced reporting: the authors openly disclose that the base-size bidirectional Mamba underperforms the Transformer across the board, that the Transformer baseline beats Mamba at utterance-level ASR, and they discuss possible explanations (scale-dependence, probing instability) with relevant citations rather than overclaiming.

Useful design guidance via ablations: the ExtBiMamba vs. InnBiMamba comparison, and the Transformer+causal-mask baseline showing that causal pre-training (not just masking at fine-tuning) matters, are genuinely informative findings.
Some statistical rigor: paired t-tests supporting the document-level vs. utterance-level WER improvement, and a parameter-matched causal comparison showing Mamba wins with 17% fewer parameters.
Clear relevance to the community: speech SSL backbones, streaming/long-context ASR, and quantized units for spoken language modeling are all of interest to ACL audiences.
weaknesses: Reproducibility gaps: the pretraining corpus is never explicitly stated (presumably LibriSpeech-960, but this must be inferred), training hyperparameters beyond step counts and batch-size ratio are not given, and there is no mention of released code or checkpoints despite models being trained from scratch.

The pretraining setup is substantially weaker than standard practice (single GPU, effective audio per batch ~1/4 of original HuBERT), so absolute numbers are far below published HuBERT baselines; while internal comparisons are fair, conclusions about Mamba as a 'speech foundation model' direction rest on a small-scale proxy that may not transfer to competitive scales - a concern partially acknowledged by the bidirectional scalability issue observed at base size.

Single-seed results for most experiments; SUPERB probing uses only four of the standard tasks and a subset score, and the authors themselves note the instability of SUPERB rankings, which weakens fine-grained claims (e.g., small-size ExtBiMamba wins with only ~1-2 point margins).

Some headline claims are overstated relative to evidence: 'first comprehensive exploration' is contestable given Zhang et al. [16] and Audio Mamba [17]; the claim that higher phone purity of quantized representations benefits spoken language modeling is asserted but never tested with an actual spoken LM downstream.

Novelty is primarily empirical rather than methodological: the architecture changes are adopted from prior work (ExtBiMamba/InnBiMamba from [10], HuBERT recipe from [9]), so the contribution hinges on the quality and generality of the experimental evidence, which is limited by the above scale issues.

Writing/format issues: the paper is in an IEEE two-column short-paper format rather than ACL style; typos remain ('probling' in Tables III/IV, 'two setting' in Sec. III); the Mamba formulation in Sec. II contains notation errors (Abar/Bbar overbar loss in Eq. 2, BroadcastD undefined).

strengths: The paper undertakes a genuinely systematic, cross-task exploration (fine-tuning for long-context and causal ASR, SUPERB-style probing, phone purity, CCA-based layer-wise analysis, and an architecture ablation), going beyond prior single-task Mamba speech studies.

The computational efficiency analysis (MACs/sec and RTF across 5s–320s inputs) is well motivated and directly supports the central claim that Mamba-based SSL scales linearly where causal Transformers OOM beyond ~80s.

Causal-setting results are reasonably convincing: Mamba variants beat causal-Transformer and masked-bidirectional baselines on PR and SUPERB_S across both base and small sizes, and the Transformer+Causal-Mask control sensibly isolates the effect of causal pretraining.
Some claims are supported with statistical testing (paired t-test for document- vs. utterance-level ASR) and multiple speaker embeddings (Resemblyzer, TitaNet, ECAPA-TDNN) to check trend robustness.
The ablation over ExtBiMamba vs. InnBiMamba, and the honest reporting that bidirectional Mamba underperforms at base scale, add useful design guidance rather than only positive results.
weaknesses: The pretraining setup is substantially weaker than standard practice (single GPU, roughly one-quarter of the original HuBERT batch audio budget), and all conclusions rest on these undertrained models; there is no comparison to official HuBERT or wav2vec 2.0 checkpoints, so it is unclear whether the observed ranking holds at realistic scale.

Key comparisons are confounded. The causal ASR result compares a 78.2M Mamba against a 94.7M Transformer without explaining how the parameter gap arose; the long-context ASR 'win' (11.08%) compares against a Transformer that OOMs, with no Transformer chunking/streaming baseline, so the gain may come from document context rather than from Mamba itself.

Multiple headline claims are overstated relative to the evidence: ExtBiMamba is actually worse than Transformer at utterance-level ASR (13.37 vs. 11.86) and at base-scale probing on all metrics; the abstract's framing of 'superior' and 'competitive' performance smooths over these negative results.

Only four SUPERB tasks are evaluated; although MiniSUPERB is cited as justification, Mamba performs worst exactly on ER and IC, tasks omitted from some comparisons, raising concern about selective framing.

Reproducibility is a serious concern: no code or model release is mentioned, pretraining details (learning rate, optimizer, hardware duration, data) are incomplete, and probing results lack seeds/variance estimates, despite the authors themselves citing SUPERB evaluation instability.
The novelty claim ('first comprehensive exploration') is weakened by prior work the authors themselves cite ([16], Zhang et al., which trains Mamba SSL and analyzes speech tasks; Audio Mamba [17]).

The paper is formatted and framed for an IEEE speech venue (ICASSP-style), and its contribution is primarily an empirical speech-architecture study with limited linguistic or NLP-methodological insight, which limits fit and impact for the ACL community.

Several analyses are descriptive only (e.g., 'possibly indicating better encoding of phonetic information') without follow-up experiments to substantiate the interpretation, and the document-level qualitative claims about rare-word consistency are anecdotal.

strengths: Systematic and fairly controlled comparison: Mamba-based and Transformer-based HuBERT models are trained from scratch under an identical (albeit reduced) setup, enabling architecture-only attributions rather than comparisons across unrelated published checkpoints.

Comprehensive coverage across settings: causal and bidirectional pretraining, fine-tuning (long-context, streaming/causal ASR), probing on four SUPERB tasks, and representation analyses (layer-wise phone purity, CCA with phoneme/speaker/emotion attributes, plus additional speaker embedders as robustness checks).

Useful efficiency analysis: MACs/sec and RTF measured across sequence lengths up to 320 seconds, clearly quantifying linear vs. quadratic scaling and the practical OOM boundary (~80s) of the causal Transformer; the document-level long-context ASR experiment (TEDLIUM3) demonstrates a capability Transformers of matched size simply cannot run.

Honest reporting of negative and mixed results: the base-size bidirectional Mamba underperforms Transformer, and the authors discuss the scale-dependence, the phone-purity vs. probing discrepancy, and cite plausible explanations rather than overclaiming.
Useful ablation on bidirectional Mamba variants (ExtBiMamba vs. InnBiMamba), including the naive Transformer + causal mask baseline that shows causal behavior must be present at pretraining time.
The analysis of quantized-representation quality (phone purity across k) connects the findings to spoken language modeling, giving the work relevance beyond pure speech ASR.
weaknesses: All models are trained at roughly one-quarter of the original HuBERT compute (single GPU, reduced total audio per batch), so the headline claims ('Mamba outperforms Transformer') hold only in this reduced-compute regime; the paper does not test whether conclusions transfer at realistic pretraining scale, and the base-size bidirectional results (PR 10.65 vs. 7.49; SUPERB_S 815 vs. 869) actively suggest they may not.

The long-context ASR advantage is largely an OOM artifact: the Transformer cannot run at document level, and Mamba's document-level WER (11.08) only marginally beats the Transformer's utterance-level WER (11.86); the paired t-test compares the same model under two conditions rather than comparing architectures, so its relevance to the claimed advantage is limited.

The causal ASR comparison confounds architecture with parameter count (78.2M vs. 94.7M); no parameter-matched Transformer baseline is provided, weakening the 'better accuracy with fewer parameters' claim.

Downstream evaluation uses only four SUPERB tasks with a nonstandard SUPERB_S aggregation; no statistical significance or variance estimates are reported for any probing or fine-tuning result, despite known instability of SUPERB rankings (which the authors themselves cite).

Reproducibility gaps: no code or model release is mentioned, and key training details (optimizer, learning rate schedule, masking configuration, data preprocessing) are underspecified; the reduced-resource recipe makes exact replication difficult.

Baselines are narrow: no comparison to Conformer or other efficient architectures, no wav2vec 2.0-style alternative, and no reference to published HuBERT numbers to contextualize absolute WERs; differentiation from Zhang et al. [16] is asserted but the incremental novelty over that concurrent analysis is not sharply demonstrated.
Several interpretive claims (e.g., that higher phone purity benefits spoken language modeling) are plausible but untested; no speech-unit LLM experiment actually validates this purported benefit.

Presentation/venue fit: the paper is in IEEE conference format, and the contribution is primarily an empirical speech-processing study; its connection to core CL/NLP questions (speech units for spoken LMs) is stated but not substantively developed.

strengths: Systematic and comprehensive empirical study: the paper covers causal and bidirectional settings, fine-tuning (long-context ASR, streaming ASR), SUPERB probing (subset plus full SUPERB in Appendix E), representation analysis (phone purity, CCA), and an ablation over bidirectional Mamba designs (ExtBiMamba vs. InnBiMamba), providing a much more unified picture than prior single-task evaluations.

Careful experimental controls: Transformer baselines are retrained from scratch under the identical (resource-constrained) setup rather than compared against official checkpoints, making architecture comparisons fair; the efficiency study reports both MACs/second and RTF averaged over runs, and long-context ASR conclusions are supported by paired t-tests.

Honest, well-scoped limitations section that explicitly acknowledges the single-GPU pretraining scale, the resulting gap to official HuBERT, and hardware-dependence of efficiency numbers, and correctly avoids overgeneralizing scaling conclusions.

Useful negative/nuanced findings: the scale-dependent behavior of bidirectional Mamba (Base underperforms Transformer, Small outperforms it), the training-instability analysis via loss-scale dynamics (Appendix D), and the observation that phone purity does not always align with probe performance add genuine analytical value beyond win/loss tables.
Direct relevance to CL/NLP interests (SSL representations, spoken language modeling inputs, streaming/long-context ASR), and codebase release supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited pretraining scale is a substantial confound: all models are trained on a single V100 with roughly one-quarter of the original batch audio, and the authors' own Transformer baseline falls well below the official FAIR HuBERT; conclusions about Mamba's competitiveness and especially its 'scalability challenges' in the bidirectional setting may not transfer to realistic pretraining regimes.

Results are from single training runs without seed variance for pretraining; given acknowledged instability of ExtBiMamba training, differences of a few points (e.g., SUPERB_S 832.31 vs. 815.38, 868.93 vs. 815.38) are hard to interpret confidently.

Novelty is incremental: Mamba-based HuBERT-style SSL models already exist (Zhang et al., 2024, 2025, which the paper itself cites and builds its ExtBiMamba/InnBiMamba definitions from); the 'first comprehensive exploration' claim is defensible only under a narrow reading of scope.

The headline causal-setting wins are partly confounded by parameter mismatch (78.2M Mamba vs. 94.7M Causal Transformer) and by the very weak 'Transformer + Causal Mask' baseline (SUPERB_S 734.68), which suggests the causal Transformer comparisons may understate Transformer performance under better causal training recipes.

Evaluation breadth is limited in the main results (4 of 10 SUPERB tasks) with full SUPERB only for a subset of models; some reported wins are narrow (e.g., Small ExtBiMamba loses IC by 5 points) and the paper's abstract-level claim of 'superior performance' overstates a mixed picture.

Presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract is missing/empty; figures (Figs. 1-3) are small and hard to read; the Introduction is dense and reads as a results summary rather than motivation; some claims (e.g., quantized representations being 'beneficial for spoken language modeling') are asserted without any SLM experiments to substantiate them.

strengths: Systematic and multi-faceted evaluation of Mamba-based HuBERT across fine-tuning (long-context, causal ASR), probing (SUPERB subset plus full SUPERB in Appendix E), and representational analyses (phone purity, CCA with phone/speaker/emotion attributes), which is more comprehensive than prior isolated-task studies of Mamba in speech
The efficiency analysis (MACs/sec and RTF across sequence lengths, with OOM boundaries) directly substantiates the core architectural motivation with measurable evidence

Honest reporting of negative results, e.g., the base-scale ExtBiMamba underperforming the Transformer bidirectionally, the utterance-level ASR gap, and the scale-dependent ablation between ExtBiMamba and InnBiMamba

The Limitations section is candid about the constrained training setup (single GPU, reduced effective batch), and the training-instability analysis (loss-scale dynamics in Appendix D) offers a plausible mechanism for the bidirectional Mamba gap
Codebase is stated to be released, and evaluation follows standard protocols (HuBERT pretraining recipe, wav2vec2 fine-tuning, SUPERB defaults), supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: The pre-training regime is severely under-resourced relative to standard HuBERT (effective batch audio ~1/4 of the original, single V100, single run with no averaging or variance estimates), so the headline claims—especially about scalability and cross-setting superiority—may not generalize to realistic training scales; the paper itself concedes its Transformer baseline scores below the official FAIR model

Several central claims are contradicted or weakened by the paper's own tables: Mamba loses to the Transformer at utterance-level ASR (13.37 vs 11.86), the base-size bidirectional Mamba underperforms across the board, and the abstract/contribution bullet 'outperforming its Transformer-based counterpart' is only true under selected conditions, which overstates the contribution

Key comparisons conflate parameter counts and architectural changes: the '17% fewer parameters' claim in causal ASR, the Mamba+MLP variant introduced ad hoc, and the inconsistent superiority of InnBiMamba vs ExtBiMamba across scales make it hard to attribute gains to Mamba itself rather than to configuration choices

No statistical treatment for most results: only one paired t-test (utterance vs document level for a single model) is reported; all SUPERB and ASR numbers come from single runs without confidence intervals

Presentation issues undermine polish: the code URL is missing in the abstract, the RTF plot in Figure 1 has a confusing/reversed-looking axis, some tables reference evaluations (e.g., SF in the SUPERB_S formulation) inconsistent with the four tasks used, and Appendix E introduces SUPERB_FULL scores that cannot be compared to SUPERB_S, fragmenting the evidence

The probing evaluation uses only a four-task subset for the main tables; while MiniSUPERB is cited as justification and a full evaluation is provided for only four models, the full evaluation partly shifts the picture (e.g., Mamba's paralinguistic/semantic weaknesses), which the main text does not fully surface
The claim of 'first comprehensive exploration' is contestable given Zhang et al. (2025) and prior Mamba speech SSL work, which the paper cites but distinguishes somewhat thinly

strengths: Systematic and comprehensive empirical study: the paper trains Mamba-based HuBERT models under causal and bidirectional settings and evaluates them across fine-tuned ASR (utterance-level, long-context document-level, causal/streaming), SUPERB probing (with a full 10-task SUPERB evaluation in Appendix E), phone purity, and CCA-based layer-wise analyses, addressing a genuine gap left by prior single-task studies of Mamba in speech.

The efficiency analysis (MACs/second and RTF across sequence lengths from 5s to 320s) concretely substantiates the linear-scaling claim, including a demonstrable practical advantage where the Transformer baseline OOMs at ~80s while Mamba fine-tunes full documents, improving WER from 13.37% to 11.08%.

Honest and informative negative results: the paper does not oversell Mamba — it clearly reports that bidirectional Mamba underperforms Transformer at Base scale, connects this to training instability with a loss-scale analysis (Figure 7), and shows the optimal bidirectional design is scale-dependent. This kind of design guidance is valuable to the community.

Strong alignment between analyses: probing results (Table 3), phone purity (Figure 2), and CCA similarity (Figure 3) tell a consistent story, and the paper appropriately qualifies cases where representational quality does not predict probe performance.
Transparent limitations section that explicitly acknowledges the single-GPU, reduced-batch training regime and the weaker Transformer baseline relative to official FAIR checkpoints.

Relevant to CL/NLP interests: the finding of higher-quality quantized representations connects to spoken language modeling and speech unit extraction, and the methodology follows well-established protocols (HuBERT pretraining, SUPERB, wav2vec2 fine-tuning).
weaknesses: All pretraining results are from a single training run without variance estimates; given that Mamba variants reportedly exhibit training instability, single-run comparisons (e.g., SUPERB_S gaps of 10-20 points) are hard to interpret, and the significance analysis is limited to one paired t-test in the long-context ASR setting.

The constrained scale (single V100, roughly one-quarter of the original HuBERT batch audio) weakens the Transformer baseline relative to known reference numbers; some conclusions (especially the bidirectional scalability limitation) may be artifacts of this budget rather than intrinsic properties, a caveat the authors acknowledge but cannot resolve.

Several results are mixed or modest: in the causal Base setting the standard Mamba loses substantially on IC (87.45 vs. 94.23) and ER, and in the bidirectional Small setting ExtBiMamba trails on IC; the headline advantage rests mainly on causal phonetic/speaker tasks and long-context efficiency.

Reproducibility is undermined by an incomplete codebase link in the abstract ('The codebase is available at' with no URL), and there is an internal inconsistency: Section 6 states the SUPERB_S subset uses PR/SID/ER/IC, while Appendix C describes the subset as PR/SID/ER/SF.

Novelty is primarily empirical: the architecture and training recipe are assembled from existing components (HuBERT recipe, ExtBiMamba/InnBiMamba from Zhang et al. 2024, Mamba implementation of Gu & Dao), and some findings (e.g., Mamba's causal/efficiency advantage) are expected from prior work on SSMs and streaming ASR.

The efficiency comparison lacks kernel-level detail and batched-inference considerations; absolute RTF/MACs are hardware-dependent, and a comparison against memory-optimized Transformer variants (e.g., flash attention with causal masking) would strengthen the claim that OOM is a fundamental limitation.
